title: Why orchestration
summary: From one docker run to a fleet: what Kubernetes takes off your hands.

steps.title: From one container to a fleet
body: You already know `docker run -d -p 8080:80 shop-api:1.4`. On one laptop that is enough. In production you soon need answers to:
- The container crashed at 3 a.m. **Who restarts it?**
- The machine died. **Who starts the container somewhere else?**
- Traffic tripled. **Who starts five more copies, and who spreads requests across them?**
- Version 1.5 is out. **Who replaces copies one at a time without downtime, and rolls back if it breaks?**
- Copies move between machines. **How do other services find them?**

A container **orchestrator** answers all of these. Kubernetes (k8s) is the one that won: you describe *what you want running*, and it keeps the world looking like that description, on as many machines as you give it.
> **Tip:** Kubernetes does not build images. You still `docker build` and push to a registry; Kubernetes pulls and runs them.

steps.prompt: Which job is **not** something Kubernetes does for you?
options: Building your container image from a Dockerfile
Moving containers off a dead machine
Spreading traffic across copies of a service
steps.explain: Images are built by Docker, BuildKit or your CI pipeline and pushed to a registry. Kubernetes only pulls and runs them.

steps.title: Inside a cluster
body: A **cluster** is a set of machines (**nodes**) plus a **control plane** that decides what runs where.
```text
|  kube-apiserver   <-- every request goes through here (kubectl)  |
|  etcd             <-- the database: the desired + observed state |
|  kube-scheduler   <-- picks a node for each new pod              |
|  controller-mgr   <-- loops that fix drift (replicas, nodes...)  |
| kubelet          |   | kubelet          |   | kubelet          |
| container runtime|   | container runtime|   | container runtime|
| kube-proxy       |   | kube-proxy       |   | kube-proxy       |
| [pod] [pod]      |   | [pod]            |   | [pod] [pod] [pod]|
- The **API server** is the only component that talks to etcd. Everything else, including `kubectl` and the kubelets, talks to the API server.
- The **kubelet** on each node watches for pods assigned to its node and asks the **container runtime** (containerd, CRI-O) to start them.
- **kube-proxy** programs the node's networking so Services work (module 3).
- A **pod** is the smallest thing Kubernetes runs: one or more containers sharing a network address.

steps.prompt: Match each component to its job.
pairs: the front door: validates and stores every change
key-value store holding the cluster state
chooses a node for each unscheduled pod
agent on each node that starts and watches its pods
runs loops that push actual state towards desired
pulls images and runs the containers

steps.explain: On managed clusters (AKS, EKS, GKE) the provider runs the control plane for you; you only see and pay for the worker nodes.

steps.prompt: The node running two of your pods loses power. What happens next, assuming the pods belong to a Deployment?
options: The control plane notices the node is gone and new pods are scheduled on the remaining nodes
Nothing until someone runs `kubectl apply` again
The kubelet on the dead node restarts them when power returns, and not before
etcd copies the containers to another node
steps.explain: The node stops sending heartbeats, the node controller marks it `NotReady`, its pods are evicted, and the ReplicaSet controller sees too few pods and creates replacements, which the scheduler places on healthy nodes. Expect a few minutes by default.

steps.prompt: Kubernetes keeps comparing what you asked for with what is running. What does this print?
steps.explain: This compare-and-correct idea is the heart of Kubernetes. The next lesson makes it precise.

steps.title: Watch a controller correct the cluster
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). The Deployment `web` wants 3 pods. Look first: `kubectl get deploy,rs,pods`.
1. Delete one of `web`'s pods and watch what happens (`kubectl get pods` a few times, or `kubectl get pods -w`, Ctrl+C
to stop). The controller notices the gap between desired and actual, and acts.
2. Change the **desired** state to 5 replicas, and wait until all 5 are ready.
3. Pods are not owned by the Deployment directly. Write the name of the object that owns `web`'s pods (its

checks.name: web wants 5 replicas and has 5 ready
checks.fail: `web` should want 5 replicas and have 5 ready. `kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5`, then `kubectl rollout status deploy/web`.

checks.name: owner.txt names the ReplicaSet
checks.fail: Not the owner. `kubectl get pod POD -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].kind} {.metadata.ownerReferences[0].name}'`.

hints: `kubectl delete pod NAME` (any `web-...` pod), then `kubectl get pods`: a new pod with a new name appears.
`kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5` changes the desired state; `kubectl rollout status deploy/web` waits.
`kubectl get pods -l app=web -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.ownerReferences[0].name}'` prints the ReplicaSet's name.
solution: kubectl delete pod $(kubectl get pods -l app=web -o name | head -n 1 | cut -d/ -f2)
steps.explain: You never started a pod yourself: you changed the desired state and the ReplicaSet controller closed the gap, both when a pod disappeared and when you asked for more. The chain Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods is visible in `ownerReferences`; the Deployment manages ReplicaSets (one per version), and each ReplicaSet manages its pods. That loop, observe and correct, is all of Kubernetes.
